protocol.instrument_name: NSW Pharmacist Practice Standards for Management of Acute Exacerbations of Mild to Moderate Atopic Dermatitis (Community Pharmacy Dermatology Service)
protocol.instrument_version: NSW Health Authority dated 28 August 2026; approved 28 August 2026
protocol.legal_basis: NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026); pharmacists must hold general registration under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law and have successfully completed the training requirements detailed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026). Approved Medicines are listed in the NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026).
protocol.supervision_model: approved pharmacist - appropriately trained approved pharmacists manage eligible patients as part of the NSW Health Authority (dated 28 August 2026); pharmacists must exercise professional discretion and judgement when applying the Practice Standards
protocol.scope_summary: NSW Health practice standards for approved pharmacists managing eligible patients (aged 2-65 inclusive) with previously medically diagnosed mild to moderate atopic dermatitis in acute exacerbation: nine approved topical medicines with site-specific corticosteroid rules, assessment flowchart, consent, eligibility and urgent/GP referral table, 14-day supply limit, 7-14 day clinical review, documentation and communication requirements.

inclusion.text: Patients must be aged between 2 years to 65 years (inclusive) to be eligible for the service.

provenance.section_heading: G. PATIENT ELIGIBILITY AND REFERRAL CRITERIA

inclusion.text: Has the patient been diagnosed with atopic dermatitis by a medical practitioner? Only patients who have previously been diagnosed with atopic dermatitis by a medical practitioner can be managed by pharmacists under these Practice Standards.
Patient presents to a participating approved pharmacist for management of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis.
The patient has no red flags, or exclusions (checked against the eligibility and referral criteria table).

Informed clinical and financial consent must be obtained from the patient (or, if relevant, a parent, guardian or other substitute decision maker prior to providing care under this Practice Standard).
Patients must be physically present in the pharmacy to be eligible for management.
Patients are required to have a consultation with an approved pharmacist before a medication can be supplied under the Authority.
To receive management for mild to moderate atopic dermatitis under this service, the patient must fulfill the eligibility requirements set out under Part G of the Practice Standards.
Pharmacists can only manage mild to moderate presentations of atopic dermatitis that has previously been diagnosed by a medical practitioner as part of these Practice Standards.
Both pruritus and rash must be present for a diagnosis of atopic dermatitis (examination: 'Itching and rash must be present').

exclusion.text: Severe or widespread or painful rash (Treat: No; Referral: Urgent: ED).
Raised purple rash that doesn't blanch (Treat: No; Referral: Urgent: ED).
Generalised erythema that covers 90% or more of the skin (this is a medical emergency and requires immediate ED referral) (Treat: No; Referral: Urgent: ED).

Signs of sepsis, systemic illness or other complications such as: fever, confusion, lethargy, tachycardia, hypotension, hypertension, clammy skin, rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, facial or peripheral oedema, headache, joint pain and/or swollen joints (Treat: No; Referral: Urgent: ED).
Blistering of the skin and mucous membranes (including mouth and eyes) (Treat: No; Referral: Urgent: ED).
Non-healing broken skin, sores, ulcers or crusts that are chronic (more than 4 weeks) (Treat: No; Referral: Urgent: ED).

Immunocompromised patients - due to underlying medical condition (e.g. transplant or GP recipients [printed as 'transplant or GP recipients'], patients with malignancies, patients receiving chemotherapy, HIV infection, uncontrolled diabetes, advanced age); due to medication taken by the patient (such as immunomodulatory therapy, prednisone therapy) (Treat: No; Referral column printed as 'Urgent: ED' with 'GP' appearing misaligned within the sub-bullets - unclear).
Significant body surface area involvement (>30% body surface area) (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
The condition is having a marked negative emotional and social effect (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
Complex presentation, such as those requiring antibiotic therapy for secondary infection. Pharmacists must not supply antibiotic therapy. (Treat: No; Referral: GP.)
The patient is below 2 years or over 65 years of age (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
The diagnosis is unclear (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
The patient has not been diagnosed with atopic dermatitis by a medical practitioner (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
Atopic dermatitis affecting the genitals (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
Pregnant or planning a pregnancy (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
Atypical presentations of atopic dermatitis (i.e. not classic atopic dermatitis) (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
A paediatric patient that presents with a history of immediate or delayed-type hypersensitivity to food, poor feeding or sleep, concerns about failure to thrive (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
Patient presents with or develops complication (e.g. eczema herpeticum) (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
There is no response to optimal treatment (within 7 days) or the condition worsens or reoccurs (Treat: No; Referral: GP).
Patient requires large quantities of topical products (such as topical corticosteroids) that require an authority from the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (Treat: No; Referral: GP).

Atopic dermatitis is often misdiagnosed as a contact irritant or allergic dermatitis. Pharmacists must be aware of potential differential diagnoses and refer these presentations for management by a medical practitioner. Only management of atopic dermatitis is permitted under these Practice Standards.
Management of the groin is beyond the scope of the Practice Standards.

provenance.section_heading: G. PATIENT ELIGIBILITY AND REFERRAL CRITERIA

steps.description: Patient presents to a participating approved pharmacist for management of mild to moderate atopic dermatitis.
Has the patient been diagnosed with atopic dermatitis by a medical practitioner? If No: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standards. Refer to GP.'

gates.criterion: Patient has been diagnosed with atopic dermatitis by a medical practitioner

steps.description: Is the patient >=2 and <=65 years old*? If No: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standards. Refer to GP.' (asterisk printed on the gate; no footnote located in the document text)

Does the patient have any red flags, or exclusions? If Yes: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standards. Refer to Emergency Department or GP.' (pharmacists must not provide management where there is a 'No' in the 'Treat' column and must take appropriate action in accordance with established referral pathways)

gates.criterion: No red flags and no exclusions under the eligibility and referral criteria table

steps.description: Obtain informed consent: Participation; Financial; Pharmacist communication with other health practitioners. If No consent: 'Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standards. Refer to GP.'

gates.criterion: Informed consent obtained (participation, financial, communication with other health practitioners)

steps.description: Conduct patient history and clinical review including review of contraindications, precautions, drug interactions, pregnancy and lactation status.
Establish management plan.
Communicate agreed management plan with patient and patient's medical practitioner. Document all aspects of management plan.

Patient history should include: Age; Weight (if a child); Pregnancy and lactation status (if applicable); Onset, duration, nature, location, severity and extent of the rash including recent or previous relapse or flare ups, and other symptoms; Previous diagnosis of atopic dermatitis and any current or past management plan; Underlying associated medical conditions including asthma, allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, allergic contact dermatitis, food allergy and depression; Details of and response to previous treatments; Impacts on quality of life and psychosocial wellbeing including sleep and learning; Dietary history and changes in diet; Exposure to potential triggers or irritants; Other factors including family history, environmental factors (e.g. exposure to smoking and airborne pollution) and infectious factors; Current, recently commenced or recently ceased medications; Allergies/adverse drug events. The My Health Record should be reviewed where appropriate and available.
Physical examination of the patient's skin is required to identify, assess and classify the severity of an acute exacerbation of atopic dermatitis. Itching and rash must be present.

gates.criterion: Itching and rash present on examination

steps.description: Severity: 'SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD) index and the Eczema Area and Severity Index (EASI) can be used to assess the severity of atopic dermatitis to determine whether the patient requires a referral and to inform the treatment plan and monitor treatment effectiveness. Use of these scoring systems are beyond the scope of these Practice Standards.' 'Conventional scoring systems may underestimate severity and erythema in people with darker skin tones including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and Pacific Islander populations, and people of African descent. Consider the skin tone when assessing erythema.'
Development of an Eczema Action Plan: Based on the Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy Action Plan for Eczema template.

Non-pharmacological/general measures: advice regarding skin care and minimising aggravating factors; advice on how to manage the itch-scratch cycle. Regular use of moisturisers (emollients) and avoiding aggravating and triggering factors are a central component of managing atopic dermatitis.

Pharmacotherapy as per the Therapeutic Guidelines using Approved Medicines only (Hydrocortisone 1% ointment; Methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% lotion, ointment or fatty ointment; Triamcinolone acetonide 0.02% ointment; Mometasone furoate 0.1% ointment; Betamethasone dipropionate 0.05% ointment; Betamethasone valerate 0.1% ointment; Desonide 0.05% lotion; Pimecrolimus 1% cream; Crisaborole 2% ointment). 'Patients should be advised that each new treatment may take time to work and should be trialled for 7 days. If there is no improvement, the patient must be referred to a medical practitioner.' 'Pharmacists must only supply formulations listed in the Authority.'

gates.criterion: Improvement after trialling the new treatment for 7 days

steps.description: Topical corticosteroid site rules: 'For management of the face, pharmacists must use hydrocortisone 1% ointment only. All stronger potency corticosteroid therapies cannot be supplied by the pharmacist under the Practice Standards and can only be prescribed by a medical practitioner.' 'For management of flexural sites, pharmacists must use hydrocortisone 1% ointment or desonide 0.05% lotion only. All stronger potency corticosteroid therapies cannot be supplied by the pharmacist under the Practice Standards and can only be prescribed by a medical practitioner.' 'Management of the groin is beyond the scope of the Practice Standards.' 'For management of the scalp in children, pharmacists can use desonide 0.05% lotion or methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% lotion only.'

gates.criterion: Face treatment uses hydrocortisone 1% ointment only
Flexural site treatment uses hydrocortisone 1% ointment or desonide 0.05% lotion only
Site of management is not the groin
Scalp treatment in children uses desonide 0.05% lotion or methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% lotion only

steps.description: 'Tar preparations can cause sensitivity reactions and are beyond the scope of these Practice Standards, and can only be initiated by a medical practitioner.' 'Treatment of infection in atopic dermatitis is beyond the scope of these Practice Standards and requires a referral to a medical practitioner.' 'Pharmacists must not supply antibiotic therapy.'

gates.criterion: No tar preparations supplied or initiated by the pharmacist
No treatment of infection (no antibiotic therapy supplied) by the pharmacist

steps.description: Counselling (comprehensive advice and counselling including supportive written information when required) regarding: Product and medication use: dosing and application instructions for topical corticosteroids, emollients, and other topical products, wet dressing use; How to manage adverse reactions; When to seek further care and/or treatment from a medical practitioner; How to recognise infection; When to return for a clinical review; How to manage the itch-scratch cycle. 'Treatment may be unsuccessful when there is poor adherence with therapy, skin infection, allergy or severe dermatitis.' 'Patients should be advised to immediately see a medical practitioner if symptoms worsen after commencing treatment.' 'When recommending topical corticosteroids for atopic dermatitis, pharmacists should reassure patients/caregivers who have concerns about the safety of topical corticosteroids that they are safe when used appropriately.'

The agreed management plan must be documented in the patient electronic clinical record and shared with members of the patient's multidisciplinary team, in accordance with the Authority. Where a patient has a My Health Record, the pharmacist must ensure the details of the supply are uploaded to My Health Record, unless requested otherwise by the patient.

Clinical review with the pharmacist should occur in line with recommendations in the Therapeutic Guidelines. Patients should be advised and educated on how and when to seek a review with medical practitioner.

Clinical review is recommended 7 to 14 days after the initiation of treatment for acute atopic dermatitis to assess: Response to treatment; Adverse effects; If changes are required to the treatment plan, decisions to continue, modify or stop treatment should be reflected in the patient's eczema action plan.

gates.criterion: Treatment for acute atopic dermatitis initiated and 7 to 14 days elapsed

steps.description: 'If a patient experiences worsening of symptoms, minimal improvement in symptoms after commencing pharmacist care, a secondary infection, they must be referred for an urgent review by a medical practitioner.'

gates.criterion: Worsening of symptoms, minimal improvement after commencing pharmacist care, or secondary infection

steps.description: If a good response has been achieved, the medication can be reduced or stopped, and the patient can continue using regular moisturiser only.

gates.criterion: Good response to therapy achieved at review

steps.description: If there has been an inadequate response to therapy due to compliance issues such as inappropriate use, or a patient not applying enough medication, the pharmacist may provide further advice.

gates.criterion: Inadequate response to therapy due to compliance issues (inappropriate use or not applying enough medication)

steps.description: Pharmacists should generally only supply a sufficient quantity of medicine (including repeats) for the period until the patient's review. Pharmacists can only supply a maximum of 14 days of therapy under these Practice Standards.

gates.criterion: Supply does not exceed a maximum of 14 days of therapy

steps.description: Pharmacotherapy for management of atopic dermatitis may be required longer-term. Pharmacists should refer patients to a medical practitioner for a review and ongoing management after the acute flare has been managed. An annual review by a medical practitioner is recommended to assess for adverse effects from topical corticosteroid therapy.

red_flags.trigger_text: Severe or widespread or painful rash
Raised purple rash that doesn't blanch
Generalised erythema that covers 90% or more of the skin (this is a medical emergency and requires immediate ED referral)

Signs of sepsis, systemic illness or other complications such as: fever, confusion, lethargy, tachycardia, hypotension, hypertension, clammy skin, rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, facial or peripheral oedema, headache, joint pain and/or swollen joints
Blistering of the skin and mucous membranes (including mouth and eyes)
Non-healing broken skin, sores, ulcers or crusts that are chronic (more than 4 weeks)

Immunocompromised patients - due to underlying medical condition (e.g. transplant or GP recipients, patients with malignancies, patients receiving chemotherapy, HIV infection, uncontrolled diabetes, advanced age); due to medication taken by the patient (such as immunomodulatory therapy, prednisone therapy)
Significant body surface area involvement (>30% body surface area)
The condition is having a marked negative emotional and social effect
Complex presentation, such as those requiring antibiotic therapy for secondary infection. Pharmacists must not supply antibiotic therapy.
The patient is below 2 years or over 65 years of age
The diagnosis is unclear
The patient has not been diagnosed with atopic dermatitis by a medical practitioner
Atopic dermatitis affecting the genitals
Pregnant or planning a pregnancy
Atypical presentations of atopic dermatitis (i.e. not classic atopic dermatitis)
A paediatric patient that presents with a history of immediate or delayed-type hypersensitivity to food, poor feeding or sleep, concerns about failure to thrive
Patient presents with or develops complication (e.g. eczema herpeticum)
There is no response to optimal treatment (within 7 days) or the condition worsens or reoccurs
Patient requires large quantities of topical products (such as topical corticosteroids) that require an authority from the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme

Secondary infection is a common complication of atopic dermatitis. If a secondary infection co-occurs in the presentation, the patient must be referred to a medical practitioner for investigation and management. Treatment of infection in atopic dermatitis is beyond the scope of these Practice Standards and requires a referral to a medical practitioner.
All severe cases of atopic dermatitis must be urgently referred to a medical practitioner for management without any treatment by the pharmacists.
Complications of atopic dermatitis - pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients for urgent medical assessment at presentation or at any stage if a complication develops.

Eczema herpeticum - 'Vesicles develop usually in areas of active or recent atopic dermatitis, followed by the onset of high fever and adenopathy ... Painful corneal lesions will develop if the eye is involved and if the HSV infection becomes systemic. This may be fatal. This is a medical emergency. Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department for urgent medical assessment.'
'Patients should be advised that each new treatment may take time to work and should be trialled for 7 days. If there is no improvement, the patient must be referred to a medical practitioner.'
Patients should be advised to immediately see a medical practitioner if symptoms worsen after commencing treatment.

Common adverse effects of topical corticosteroids such as transient burning, stinging or pain on application can generally be reversed by stopping the medication. Referral to a medical practitioner is required if the adverse effect does not resolve quickly.

All patients should be advised to contact a medical practitioner if: They are not responding to treatment (within 7 days); Their signs and symptoms worsen; They are experiencing complications (as soon as they become evident); They are having unmanageable adverse effects

If a patient experiences worsening of symptoms, minimal improvement in symptoms after commencing pharmacist care, a secondary infection, they must be referred for an urgent review by a medical practitioner.

If the treating pharmacist becomes aware of an uncommon, unexpected or serious adverse event following treatment with an Approved Medicine, this should be reported to the Therapeutic Goods Administration ... Additionally, you must notify the patient's usual general practitioner (if they have one).

routine: Patients who have requested the service but are not eligible for management should be referred to their regular medical practitioner or health service.
Pharmacists must apply clinical judgement and refer any patient considered appropriate for medical care.
If a secondary infection co-occurs in the presentation, the patient must be referred to a medical practitioner for investigation and management.
Pharmacists should refer patients to a medical practitioner for a review and ongoing management after the acute flare has been managed.

Atopic dermatitis is often misdiagnosed as a contact irritant or allergic dermatitis. Pharmacists must be aware of potential differential diagnoses and refer these presentations for management by a medical practitioner.
urgent: Patients who meet any of the urgent referral criteria below must be referred to their regular medical practitioner, maternity provider, health service, or Emergency Department (ED) as indicated in the table.
Patients presenting with generalised erythema that covers 90% of the skin require urgent referral to a medical practitioner.
All severe cases of atopic dermatitis must be urgently referred to a medical practitioner for management without any treatment by the pharmacists.
Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients for urgent medical assessment at presentation or at any stage if a complication develops.
they must be referred for an urgent review by a medical practitioner.
emergency: Generalised erythema that covers 90% or more of the skin (this is a medical emergency and requires immediate ED referral).
This may be fatal. This is a medical emergency. Pharmacists are required to immediately refer these patients to an emergency department for urgent medical assessment. (eczema herpeticum)
Not eligible for management under the Authority and Practice Standards. Refer to Emergency Department or GP. (flowchart, red flags/exclusions = Yes)

review_followup.when: 7 to 14 days after the initiation of treatment for acute atopic dermatitis
review_followup.what: Clinical review to assess response to treatment, adverse effects, and if changes are required to the treatment plan (decisions to continue, modify or stop treatment should be reflected in the patient's eczema action plan).

review_followup.when: In line with recommendations in the Therapeutic Guidelines
review_followup.what: Clinical review with the pharmacist; patients should be advised and educated on how and when to seek a review with medical practitioner.

review_followup.when: When a good response has been achieved
review_followup.what: The medication can be reduced or stopped, and the patient can continue using regular moisturiser only.

review_followup.when: After the acute flare has been managed
review_followup.what: Pharmacists should refer patients to a medical practitioner for a review and ongoing management.
An annual review by a medical practitioner is recommended to assess for adverse effects from topical corticosteroid therapy.

review_followup.when: Within a week following the consultation (if the patient or substituted decision maker consents to disclosure)
review_followup.what: The record of the consultation and any subsequent consultations (including adverse events) must be shared with the patient's usual treating medical practitioner or medical practice, where the patient has one.

conditions: If the treating pharmacist becomes aware of an uncommon, unexpected or serious adverse event following treatment with an Approved Medicine, this should be reported to the Therapeutic Goods Administration. This should be conducted via the usual processes, by reporting online at https://aems.tga.gov.au/.
Additionally, you must notify the patient's usual general practitioner (if they have one).
Where a patient has a My Health Record, the pharmacist must ensure the details of the supply are uploaded to My Health Record, unless requested otherwise by the patient.

open_questions.topic: Asterisk on the age gate has no located footnote
open_questions.observed: Flowchart gate reads 'Is the patient >=2 and <=65 years old*' with an asterisk; no footnote or explanatory note for the asterisk was found anywhere in the extracted text (16 pages).
open_questions.why_unclear: The asterisk may point to a qualification (e.g. exception for certain patients) that is not present in the text; gate transcribed without the qualification and confidence marked medium.

open_questions.topic: Flowchart box order reconstructed from diagram layout
open_questions.observed: Section D flowchart text is interleaved, e.g. 'Is the patient >=2 and <=65 years old* No under the Authority and Practice' and Yes/No branch labels appear detached from boxes.
open_questions.why_unclear: Step order and on_fail assignments were inferred from the diagram layout; branch wording transcribed verbatim. Confidence medium on PW-1-S4.

open_questions.topic: Referral table headers reversed/mirrored in extraction
open_questions.observed: Above the table rows the text reads 'sngis gninraw 'gafl deR'' (the heading "'Red flag' warning signs" reversed) and mid-table 'fo sliateD gnitneserp tnialpmoc' ('Details of presenting complaint' reversed), alongside the header 'Referral criteria Treat Referral'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Column alignment of the table cannot be fully confirmed from the extraction; rows transcribed with Treat: No and Referral (Urgent: ED / GP) as printed per row.

open_questions.observed: Row reads 'Immunocompromised patients No Urgent: ED' and the following sub-bullet lines contain a stray 'GP' ('due to underlying medical condition (e.g. transplant or GP recipients...'), so the Referral value may be 'Urgent: ED' or 'GP'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Row alignment is ambiguous; EXC-7/RF-7 confidence marked unclear and both readings recorded (Urgent: ED on the row line; GP appearing within the sub-bullets).

open_questions.topic: Likely typo in the immunocompromised row
open_questions.observed: 'transplant or GP recipients' printed where 'transplant or graft recipients' is likely intended.
open_questions.why_unclear: Transcribed verbatim as printed; interpretation flagged rather than silently corrected.

open_questions.observed: Table rows EXC-1 to EXC-14 are printed on page 5 and EXC-15 to EXC-20 continue on page 6 without a repeated heading.
open_questions.why_unclear: Provenance uses the page on which each row appears; heading carried over from the table header on page 5.

open_questions.topic: Dose, frequency, duration and application instructions not printed
open_questions.observed: Nine approved medicines are listed with form and strength only; the document states 'Pharmacists need to refer to the Therapeutic Guidelines and the Australian Medicines Handbook for details on management' and directs to sources for potency/formulation selection.
open_questions.why_unclear: dose, frequency and duration fields left empty rather than invented; must be sourced from Therapeutic Guidelines/AMH before go-live.

open_questions.topic: No first-line designation or potency ranking printed
open_questions.observed: The nine approved medicines are listed alphabetically with no ranking; 'Selecting the correct potency and formulation of topical corticosteroids is important ... Pharmacists should consult the Therapeutic Guidelines ... and other relevant sources.'
open_questions.why_unclear: first_line set to false for all treatments; no agent is designated first-line and no potency hierarchy is printed.

open_questions.topic: Site restrictions worded only for topical corticosteroids
open_questions.observed: Face/flexural/groin/scalp rules refer to corticosteroid therapies and named agents; the document does not state whether pimecrolimus 1% cream and crisaborole 2% ointment may be used on the face, flexural sites, groin or children's scalp.
open_questions.why_unclear: Cannot extend corticosteroid site rules to the non-corticosteroid approved medicines without inventing a restriction; recorded in treatment notes as unstated.

open_questions.topic: Emollients/moisturisers are central to management but not in the Approved Medicines list
open_questions.observed: 'Regular use of moisturisers (emollients) ... are a central component of managing atopic dermatitis' and 'the patient can continue using regular moisturiser only', yet the Approved Medicines list contains only the nine listed agents.
open_questions.why_unclear: The document does not say whether moisturiser supply under this service is permitted outside the Authority's approved formulations; no treatment row was created for moisturisers.

open_questions.observed: TGA reporting and notification of the patient's usual general practitioner wording is on page 2; My Health Record upload requirement is on pages 10-11.
open_questions.why_unclear: Shared provenance uses the first page (2) per spec; range recorded here.

open_questions.observed: referral.routine quotes from pages 4, 5, 6 and 11; urgent quotes from pages 5, 7 and 11; emergency from pages 5, 8 and 3.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires one shared provenance object for the referral block using the first page; page range recorded here.

open_questions.topic: Branch actions not stated for several follow-up gates
open_questions.observed: PW-4-S2, PW-4-S5 and PW-4-S7 use on_fail 'unclear'; the follow-up section is prose and does not state actions when the review is not attended, when non-compliance is not the cause, or before the acute flare is managed.
open_questions.why_unclear: Spec requires 'unclear' plus an open question where the document does not dictate the branch; PW-4-S3/S4 on_fail branches were inferred from bullet order (confidence medium on PW-4-S4).

open_questions.topic: Flowchart gate 'diagnosed with atopic dermatitis by a medical practitioner' and exclusion row duplicate
open_questions.observed: The same requirement appears as a flowchart gate (page 3), an exclusion row (page 5) and a background statement (page 6).
open_questions.why_unclear: Recorded once as INC-2 (inclusion/gate) and once as EXC-13 (table row) because both are printed; the engine should treat them as the same underlying requirement.
